title: Rethinking the Crucifixion
summary: This part tackles a second “sacred cow”: the Western habit of viewing the cross mainly as an occasion for guilt over killing Jesus. From John 16, the series argues that Jesus framed His death as a birth whose pain is quickly forgotten in joy. The cross is therefore the triumphant death of the last Adam, in whom all distorted humanity died: He died not merely for us but as us. Using the woman caught in adultery, teaching on conscience and its effect on the body, and Heb 9–10, it argues that seeing Jesus like an animal sacrifice keeps believers sin-conscious and stuck in dead works. A conscience cleansed once for all frees them for the good works ordained before creation. It ends by claiming that Gentiles were never under the Mosaic law, so the blood-sacrifice aspect was a Jewish requirement, while the cross’s wider purpose was to destroy every enemy and include humanity in the resurrection.
thesis: The cross is meant to be celebrated as the once-for-all death of the old Adamic humanity, not mourned as a cause of guilt, because how we see the crucifixion determines whether our conscience is guilty or cleansed, and the conscience in turn governs our whole life, body included.

flow.step: The church’s view vs heaven’s view
flow.text: The usual Western way of seeing the cross keeps humanity condemned. Jesus’ own description in John 16 points to brief sorrow followed by lasting joy.
Like a woman in labor, the disciples would grieve for a moment and then rejoice for good. That sorrow belonged to the original witnesses, not to the post-resurrection church.

flow.step: Guilt is the antithesis of the gospel
flow.text: Treating Jesus’ death like the blood of bulls and goats leaves people forever guilty of His blood and striving to earn.
All humanity was in Christ when He died, so everything Adam made us died with Him. He died as us, once for all, and the death is as victorious as the resurrection.
With the woman caught in adultery, Jesus condemns no one. The accusers’ own consciences drive them away, while the guilty woman stays close to Him.
Conscience is the message your spirit truly believes, and that message governs the body, as the marriage-intimacy example shows. Creation waits for sons whose belief and embodiment match.
Old-covenant gifts and sacrifices could not perfect the conscience. Offering a sacrifice to become something is itself a confession of guilt and separation.

God did not want sacrifice and offering but the incarnation: God’s visible image in a body. Christ entered once for all, which means sufficient and inclusive, and His blood cleanses the conscience from dead works.
Good works were ordained before creation; dead works try to grasp what you already are. A guilty conscience traps you in dead works.
God gives you His own righteousness and glory, His opinion of Himself to hold of yourself. Scripture tells you to think of yourself as equal with God.
Conscience is seared, guilty or cleansed. Peter and the Samaritan woman show conscience creating distance, and Jesus overcoming it.

The church exists to bring people to Christ’s full stature through fivefold ministry. A counterfeit fivefold of dark powers works through doctrine, teaching that death is your savior and you are still guilty.
A true sacrifice makes worshipers perfect and removes consciousness of sins. Repeated sacrifice and guilt-centred religion only remind people of sin.
The law of Moses was made with Jews, so Gentiles were never guilty under it. The cross was mainly about destroying every enemy and including all humanity in Christ’s resurrection and throne.

teachings.title: How you see the cross affects your conscience
teachings.body: The series takes on a second sacred cow: the common view of the crucifixion. The way the church has chosen to see the cross, as opposed to heaven’s view, keeps condemning people and can breed death instead of life.

teachings.title: Jesus framed His death as childbirth
teachings.body: In John 16 Jesus says His disciples will weep while the world rejoices, but their sorrow will turn to joy, like a mother who forgets labor pains once her child is born. No one will take that joy away, and they will ask the Father in His name and receive, so their joy is full. The cross was meant to hurt briefly and bring lasting joy.

teachings.title: Written for you, not to you
teachings.body: The sorrow Jesus predicted was addressed to disciples who would watch their teacher murdered. The Bible is written for us but not always to us, so the post-resurrection church should not take on the grieving posture of Good Friday.

teachings.title: Guilt over killing Jesus is the opposite of the gospel
teachings.body: Western teaching often makes people feel guilty for killing Jesus so they will rush to the altar and repent. The series calls this the antithesis of the gospel. If Jesus’ sacrifice is reduced to the blood of bulls and goats, you live guilty of His blood instead of freed by His resurrection, and you can only keep earning and striving.

teachings.title: The cross was humanity’s most victorious moment
teachings.body: The death, burial and resurrection of Jesus was the most magnificent victory humanity has seen. The one who died at Calvary was the distorted form of all humanity, so it was a death to be celebrated.

teachings.title: The last Adam: no more Adams, only Christ
teachings.body: “As in Adam all die” was fulfilled at the cross, where everyone in Adam died. Jesus was the last Adam, so there are no more Adams, only Christ. All humanity was included in Him, and what died was everything you were never meant to be.

teachings.title: The same Spirit gives life to your mortal body
teachings.body: Had we grasped the cross, we would have applauded at its foot that everything Adam said we were was going to the grave. The Spirit who raised Christ now lives in believers and gives life to their mortal bodies.

teachings.title: He died as you, not just for you
teachings.body: Films and worship songs about the cross are moving, but they take a natural view of something supernatural. Saying only “I can’t believe You died for me” misses the message: He died as you, once for all, sufficiently and inclusively.

teachings.title: “Appointed to die once” answered
teachings.body: When people point out that humans are appointed to die once, the series answers that believers already died that death with Christ.

teachings.title: Seeking someone to pay for Jesus’ death misses who He is
teachings.body: The Crusades are cited as a dark moment when Christians wanted someone to pay for Jesus’ death. Yet Jesus said no one takes His life from Him; He laid it down.

teachings.title: The cross as one simultaneous victory
teachings.body: How you perceive the cross decides whether your conscience is cleansed or guilty. Seeing the last Adam put to death so all humanity could share in one victory, we would applaud the death as much as the resurrection. Sin was taken out in the grave, life was seated on the throne, and believers were part of both.

teachings.title: Judgment happens, but God doesn’t do it
teachings.body: In the account of the woman caught in adultery, Jesus later says He judges no one. Judgment does take place, but not by God: Jesus simply invites anyone without sin to throw the first stone, and the accusers’ own consciences condemn them.

teachings.title: Oldest to youngest: striving deepens condemnation
teachings.body: The accusers left from the oldest to the youngest. The sermon explains that the longer you spend trying to become what you already are, the more condemned your conscience becomes.

teachings.title: Ignorance is better than legalism
teachings.body: The accusers were near the Creator and welcome, yet they left, as Adam hid after trying to become like God. The woman caught in the act stayed close because of her ignorance. Prostitutes and tax collectors enter the kingdom first, and the scribes and Pharisees shut it for themselves and others.

teachings.title: Proximity isn’t about behavior
teachings.body: Some will stay near Jesus and some will leave, and the choice is ours. Behavior does not decide it: the most outwardly righteous walked away, and the one caught in sin stayed.

teachings.title: “Go and sin no more” as prophetic declaration
teachings.body: Jesus asks whether anyone condemned her and says neither does He. The sermon reads hamartia (sin) as “distorted form”, so “sin no more” is not an instruction but a prophetic declaration that she was now whole, with everything she was never meant to be removed.

teachings.title: Echoing the light of life
teachings.body: Jesus then says that whoever follows Him will not walk in darkness but will “have” the light of life. The sermon renders “have” as “echo”: a perfect copy of His light.

teachings.title: Conscience is your spirit’s authentic message
teachings.body: How you see yourself determines what you will receive from Jesus, and your paradigm frames your experience. The sermon says conscience appears 32 times in the New Testament, from every author. The key difference between animal sacrifices and Jesus was their effect on the conscience. Conscience is the faculty of the spirit that speaks the message you truly believe.

teachings.title: Profession without belief leaves the body enslaved
teachings.body: If you profess life well but do not truly grant yourself righteousness, your body stays a slave to your soul. Immortality depends on governing from within.

teachings.title: Sense-governed living makes you susceptible to death
teachings.body: When you become driven by the senses, you become open to death. Looking for evidence of immortality keeps you dead, because immortality is your nature, not something to pursue. When Adam and Eve’s eyes were opened they became ruled by experience, and reading the future only through the past breeds hopelessness, depression and anxiety.

teachings.title: The internal message governs biology
teachings.body: Whatever you believe within, good or bad, is passed on to your mortal body. The marriage example: a woman whose experience of men has been harmful may have a stress response instead of an arousal response, which hinders intimacy. Her inner belief must change for her biology to change.

teachings.title: Creation awaits manifest sons, not just positional ones
teachings.body: The body is our only gate to creation. Creation is not waiting for sons of God by position or confession but for sons who are manifest. That is when who God says you are, who you believe you are and what creation meets in you are one and the same, which requires escaping a guilty or seared conscience.

teachings.title: Sacrifices could not perfect the conscience
teachings.body: Heb 9 describes priests in the first tent and the high priest entering yearly with blood for sins of ignorance. The way into the holiest was not yet open, and gifts and sacrifices could not perfect the worshiper’s conscience. They were outward rules imposed until the time of reformation.

teachings.title: To offer a sacrifice is to confess separation
teachings.body: The moment you offer a sacrifice you are confessing that you are guilty and separated. Doing in order to become is itself separation, and it is impossible to grasp life by chasing it.

teachings.title: Sacrifice and offering You did not desire
teachings.body: God said He did not desire sacrifice and offering, yet Western religion is built on them. The verse continues that a body was prepared for Him: God ordained the incarnation, the Son as the express image of the Father in a body. God likewise ordained our incarnation, to live out what was written about us before creation.

teachings.title: Once for all: sufficient and inclusive
teachings.body: Christ came as High Priest through a greater tabernacle and entered the Most Holy Place by His own blood, once for all, obtaining eternal redemption. The series reads “once” as sufficient and “for all” as including everyone. If animal blood purified the flesh, Christ’s blood, offered through the eternal Spirit, cleanses the conscience from dead works.

teachings.title: Dead works vs good works
teachings.body: Works are not bad; there are dead works and good works. Good works were prepared for us before the foundation of the world. Without a cleansed conscience your works are dead, because they try to grasp what you already are, and that kills you.

teachings.title: Christ mediates the new covenant by death
teachings.body: Christ mediates the new covenant through a death that redeems transgressions under the first covenant, so the called receive the eternal inheritance. Seeing Jesus only as a sacrifice for wrongdoing, rather than as your own death, burial and resurrection, keeps the conscience guilty and cuts you off from good works.

teachings.title: Righteousness is a matter of conscience
teachings.body: God does not make you a separate approved righteousness; He gives you His own righteousness and glory. In the series’ terms, that is His own opinion of Himself, given for you to hold toward yourself.

teachings.title: Think of yourself as equal with God
teachings.body: The sermon says people accept the message of immortality more readily than equality with God. It cites Paul’s call to have Christ’s mind, which did not count equality with God robbery, and says believers should think of themselves as equal with God. God demands this, because creation is redeemed only when believers stop playing small.

teachings.title: Conscience creates perceived distance
teachings.body: Peter fell at Jesus’ knees and begged Him to depart because he was sinful. God never separates from you and will never leave you, but conscience can make you feel far away.

teachings.title: Three conditions of conscience
teachings.body: A cleansed conscience believes you are everything He is and nothing He is not. A guilty conscience is still under religion, striving to close a gap of perceived separation. A seared conscience refuses to hear the message, and searing it shipwrecks faith.

teachings.title: Jesus overcomes a guilty conscience
teachings.body: The Samaritan woman had had five husbands and was living with a man who was not her husband. Jesus revealed that He knew all this and still offered her life. Her joy was that He knew everything and offered heaven anyway; she left her water jar and told the town.

teachings.title: The church is a training organization
teachings.body: The local church exists to bring believers to the full stature of Christ. It is not a social or charitable organization but a place of training, and God’s structure for it is the fivefold ministry of apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers.

teachings.title: A counterfeit fivefold works through doctrine
teachings.body: Scripture also names a parallel order of dark powers: principalities, powers, mights, dominions, high things and rulers in high places, each counterfeiting a fivefold office. Rulers in high places mirror the apostolic voice. Demons are responsible not for destruction but for doctrine, and their ideal message is that death is your savior and you are still guilty.

teachings.title: A sacrifice aims at perfection, not improvement
teachings.body: The law was a shadow, not the reality, and its yearly sacrifices could never make worshipers perfect. A sacrifice’s goal is perfection, not improvement. Hebrews presents Jesus as a better Moses and a better covenant, and warns against treating His sacrifice like its shadow, which would imply you did wrong and something must die in your place.

teachings.title: Gentiles were never under the law of Moses
teachings.body: God names the parties to each covenant. The law was made with Jews, so it never applied to Gentiles, and they were never guilty under it. The series says, apologizing in advance, that the blood-sacrifice aspect was not required for Gentiles: it was a necessary but small part of a Jewish system that satisfied the law’s righteous requirement for Jews.

teachings.title: The point of the cross: destroy every enemy, include all
teachings.body: The cross’s real purpose was to destroy every enemy humanity would face and draw all humanity into the resurrection. Rather than covering misdeeds with blood, it put you into Adam to die your death so that you are now with Jesus on His throne at God’s right hand.

teachings.title: A good sacrifice ends sacrifices
teachings.body: If the sacrifices had worked they would have stopped, because worshipers once purified would have no more consciousness of sins. Sin-consciousness is the kindergarten of faith; believing His death was once for all leaves only righteousness and life.

teachings.title: Religion as a yearly reminder of sin
teachings.body: Those sacrifices were a yearly reminder of sin, so a sacrificial religion affirms guilt and never removes it. If Jesus’ sacrifice is reduced to animal blood, you stay guilty and church becomes the worst thing for your conscience.

teachings.title: Religion harms what Jesus welcomes
teachings.body: Many Western churchgoers attend to hear that they are guilty and killed an innocent man. Broken people thrown at Jesus’ feet find He does not condemn them, and they stay that way until a religious person gets hold of them. The next session, “The Day Death Died”, is announced.

stories.title: The woman in labor
stories.text: Jesus compares the coming crucifixion to childbirth: hours of pain and years of joy, with the pain forgotten. The point is that the cross was meant to produce lasting joy, not lasting guilt.

stories.title: Moving films and worship songs
stories.text: The preacher admits he cries at films and songs about the cross, but calls them a natural view of something supernatural. Lingering on “You died for me” misses that He died as us.

stories.title: “Appointed to die once”
stories.text: The preacher recalls how often people quote the verse about dying once at him, and he answers that believers already died with Christ.

stories.title: The Crusades
stories.text: He describes the Crusades as an awful episode in which Christians wanted someone to pay for Jesus’ death. That is a sign they misunderstood a Savior who said no one takes His life from Him.

stories.title: The woman caught in adultery
stories.text: The religious leaders throw a woman at Jesus’ feet and cite Moses. He invites the sinless to throw first, and they leave, oldest first, condemned by their own consciences. He tells her He does not condemn her either. Ignorance kept her close to the Creator while legalism drove the respectable away.

stories.title: Adam hiding in the garden
stories.text: When God came for His walk in the cool of the day, Adam hid because he had tried to become like God and had died. He is paired with the accusers in John 8 as people who withdrew from God’s presence.

stories.title: Newlyweds and the body
stories.text: The pastor and his wife counsel newly married couples who are disappointed with intimacy. A woman whose past makes her believe masculinity is dangerous may have a stress response rather than arousal. This illustrates that inner belief governs biology.

stories.title: God’s gift registry
stories.text: Jesus, the preacher jokes, went to the gift registry and listed the only two things He did not want: sacrifice and offering. What He wanted was a body prepared for Him, the incarnation.

stories.title: Peter at Jesus’ knees
stories.text: After the miraculous catch, Peter begged Jesus to leave because he was sinful. Jesus had not moved away; Peter’s conscience made him feel distant.

stories.title: The woman at the well
stories.text: Jesus told the Samaritan woman everything about her five husbands and current partner and still offered her living water. She left her water jar and told the town about the man who knew everything about her. This shows Jesus overcoming a guilty conscience.

stories.title: The person under the bridge
stories.text: A broken addict brought to Jesus is usually fine, because Jesus does not condemn. The damage starts when a religious person gets hold of them, and the preacher says they would have been better left alone.

words.claimed: “Ha-morphē”: a distorted form; so “sin no more” declares the woman whole rather than commanding her.
words.lexicon: Sin or a wrong act; from hamartanō, to miss the mark or err (BDAG/LSJ). It has no link to morphē (form); a popular etymology splits it into a- (not) plus meros (part), but that is also folk etymology. In John 8:11 “sin no more” is the present imperative (mēketi hamartane), a command.

words.claimed: “Have” means “echo”: a perfect carbon copy of the light of life.
words.lexicon: Echō means to have, hold or possess. The English “echo” comes from a different Greek word, ēchō (sound), which is unrelated in meaning. The verse says the follower will possess the light of life.

words.claimed: “Once” means sufficient and “for all” means inclusive of everyone.
words.lexicon: Once for all time, once and never again (BDAG). It stresses the finality and sufficiency of the single offering, not the number of people included. Inclusiveness is argued elsewhere (2 Cor 5:14; 1 John 2:2), not from this word.

words.claimed: The faculty of the spirit that speaks what you truly believe; it appears 32 times in the NT, used by every author.
words.lexicon: Consciousness or conscience, moral awareness of oneself (BDAG). It occurs about 30–32 times, mainly in Paul, Hebrews, 1 Peter and Acts, plus a disputed reading in John 8:9. It is not in Matthew, Mark, Luke, James, Jude or Revelation, so “every author” is wrong; the definition is a reasonable theological paraphrase.

questions.q: How did Jesus Himself describe the emotional meaning of His crucifixion in John 16?
questions.a: As childbirth: real but brief sorrow, then a joy that is permanent and that no one can take away. The series concludes that the church should look at the cross with celebration rather than ongoing guilt.

questions.q: What is the difference between saying “He died for me” and “He died as me”?
questions.a: “For me” can leave the believer outside the event, guilty that an innocent man died in their place. “As me” means all humanity was in the last Adam, so the old self died with Him once for all, and believers share both His death and His resurrection.

questions.q: Why did the accusers leave and the woman stay in John 8?
questions.a: Jesus condemned no one; their own consciences did. The legalists, the oldest and most practiced at striving, had the most condemned consciences and withdrew, while the woman’s lack of religious striving let her stay close to Jesus.

questions.q: What are the three conditions of conscience, and which one does the gospel produce?
questions.a: Seared (refusing the message), guilty (still striving to close a perceived gap) and cleansed (believing you are everything He is and nothing He is not). Christ’s blood, understood as a once-for-all death, produces a cleansed conscience.

questions.q: According to Hebrews 9–10 as taught here, why does a sacrifice-centred religion keep people guilty?
questions.a: Offering a sacrifice confesses guilt and separation, and repeated sacrifices are a yearly reminder of sins. A sacrifice that truly worked would make worshipers perfect and remove sin-consciousness, which is what Christ’s once-for-all offering does.

questions.q: How does conscience affect the body, according to the series?
questions.a: The message you truly believe, good or bad, is passed on to your mortal body, as the example of fear blocking marital intimacy shows. The body is our gate to creation, so belief and embodiment must match for believers to be manifest sons.

questions.q: What does the series say the main purpose of the cross was for Gentiles?
questions.a: Not to satisfy a law they were never under, but to destroy every enemy humanity would face and include all people in Christ’s death and resurrection, seating them with Him at God’s right hand.

practice: Celebrate the cross as victory; stop approaching it mainly as a reason to feel guilty for killing Jesus.
Confess “He died as me”, and reckon your old Adamic self as dead and buried with Him.
Ask Christ’s once-for-all work to cleanse your conscience, and drop sin-consciousness as the kindergarten of faith.
Stay close to Jesus when you fail, like the woman in John 8, instead of hiding or walking away.
Check whether you actually grant yourself the righteousness you profess, since your inner message shapes your body.
Pursue the good works ordained for you before creation, not dead works done to earn identity.
Treat the local church as a training ground toward Christ’s full stature, and screen teaching that makes death your savior or keeps you guilty.
Do not drive broken people back into condemnation; let them meet a Jesus who does not condemn.

fair.claim: Gentiles were never guilty, and Jesus’ blood sacrifice meant nothing to them; it was required only for Jews.
fair.note: This contradicts much of the New Testament. Paul argues that Jews and Gentiles alike are under sin: Gentiles have God’s law written on their hearts and will be judged by it, and all have sinned. Gentiles who were far off are said to be brought near by the blood of Christ, and the blood is described as ransoming people from every nation. Jesus is the atoning sacrifice for the sins of the whole world. Charitable reading: Gentiles were never under the Mosaic covenant as such (Rom 2:14; Eph 2:12), and the cross achieves more than covering sins, including victory over powers and union with Christ.

fair.claim: Jesus did not want sacrifice and offering, and religion built on sacrifice contradicts Him.
fair.note: Hebrews 10 quotes Ps 40 to show that Christ’s self-offering replaces animal sacrifices, not that sacrifice is unwanted. It says we are made holy “through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all”, and that He offered one sacrifice for sins forever. Ephesians calls Christ an offering and sacrifice to God. The New Testament still calls believers to living sacrifices and sacrifices of praise. Charitable reading: God never wanted ritual as a substitute for obedient, embodied life (1 Sam 15:22; Hos 6:6), and Christ’s one offering ends all others.

fair.claim: “Go and sin no more” is not an instruction but a prophetic declaration that she was perfect, based on hamartia meaning “distorted form”.
fair.note: Grammatically it is a present imperative command (mēketi hamartane), as in John 5:14, and hamartia does not mean “distorted form” (see the word study). Most scholars also note that John 7:53–8:11 is missing from the earliest manuscripts, though many accept it as an authentic tradition. Charitable reading: Jesus’ refusal to condemn comes first, and the call to a new life flows from that acceptance rather than earning it.

fair.claim: Judgment happens, but God does not do it; Jesus judges no one.
fair.note: John 8:15 must be read alongside John 8:16 (“yet if I do judge, My judgment is true”), John 5:22 and 5:27 (the Father has given all judgment to the Son), and Acts 17:31. Charitable reading: in John, Jesus came to save rather than condemn in His first coming (John 3:17; 12:47), and people often judge themselves by rejecting the light (John 3:18–19).

fair.claim: Heb 9:27 (“appointed to die once”) is answered by having died with Christ, implying believers need not physically die.
fair.note: In context Heb 9:27 compares Christ’s single death with humanity’s single death followed by judgment; it is not about spiritual co-death. Mainstream teaching holds that union with Christ’s death (Rom 6) is real and spiritual, while physical death remains until the resurrection, except for those alive at His return. Rom 8:11 is commonly read as future bodily resurrection. Charitable reading: for believers physical death is no longer the penalty or the master (1 Cor 15:55–57; Heb 2:15).

fair.claim: “He didn’t die for you; He died as you.”
fair.note: The New Testament says both. Christ died “for” (hyper) us as our substitute, and “one died for all, therefore all died”, which is representative and inclusive. Most traditions hold substitution and participation together rather than setting them against each other. Charitable reading: the series stresses the neglected participatory side (Rom 6:6; Gal 2:20).

fair.claim: The one who died on Calvary was the distorted form of all humanity.
fair.note: Scripture keeps Christ personally sinless and “without blemish” while saying God made Him “to be sin” for us and condemned sin in the likeness of sinful flesh. Mainstream theology says He bore humanity’s sin; He did not become distorted Himself. Charitable reading: the old humanity in Adam was crucified with Him (Rom 6:6).

fair.claim: Believers should think of themselves as equal with God (Phil 2:5–6).
fair.note: In Phil 2 equality with God is the pre-existent Christ’s own status, and the “mind” believers are to share is His humility in not exploiting it and emptying Himself (Phil 2:3–8). Mainstream teaching affirms union with Christ, sharing in the divine nature and joint heirship, but keeps the Creator–creature distinction. Charitable reading: the series means believers should fully accept the identity, righteousness and glory God gives in Christ rather than “playing small” (John 17:22; 1 John 4:17).

fair.claim: Demons are responsible not for destruction but for doctrine, operating as a counterfeit fivefold ministry.
fair.note: 1 Tim 4:1 does speak of “teachings of demons”, but Scripture also links the devil to destruction and affliction: the thief steals, kills and destroys, and Jesus healed those oppressed by the devil. Matching each power in Eph 6:12 to a fivefold office is speculative, and the lists in Eph 1:21, Eph 6:12 and Col 1:16 vary. Charitable reading: deception is the enemy’s main strategy (John 8:44; 2 Cor 11:3–4).

fair.claim: Fear trains a woman’s body into a parasympathetic state, with adrenal rather than ovarian responses.
fair.note: The physiology is reversed: fear and stress responses are sympathetic (fight or flight, adrenal), while sexual arousal is largely parasympathetic. The ovaries are not the main mediators of arousal. Charitable reading: the broader point is sound, since trauma and inner beliefs affect sexual response (as recognized in conditions like vaginismus) and healing beliefs can change bodily responses.

fair.claim: Conscience is mentioned 32 times in the NT by every author.
fair.note: Syneidēsis occurs about 30–32 times, depending on manuscripts, but it is absent from Matthew, Mark, Luke, James, Jude and Revelation. The count is roughly right, but “every author” is not.

fair.claim: The Crusaders wanted someone to pay for Jesus’ death.
fair.note: Historically the Crusades’ main stated aims were recovering Jerusalem and the holy places, helping Byzantium, and penance. However, anti-Jewish massacres in 1096 did use the “Christ-killer” charge, so the claim fits part of what happened. The sermon is right that they betrayed the spirit of Jesus, who laid down His own life.

fair.claim: The accusers left oldest first because longer striving produces a more condemned conscience; prostitutes enter the kingdom “before you” because of ignorance.
fair.note: The text records the order but gives no reason, so this explanation is homiletical speculation; others suggest greater age brought more self-awareness or seniority. In Matt 21:31–32 the tax collectors and prostitutes enter first because they believed John and repented, not because of ignorance.

fair.claim: Good works prepared before the foundation of the world are in “Ephesians 4”; the Samaritan woman “threw away” her water jar because she believed.
fair.note: The good-works verse is Eph 2:10 (“prepared beforehand”). John 4:28 says she left her jar, and reading it as a sign of faith is a common devotional interpretation, not the text’s own explanation. The “seventh man” remark is the preacher’s paraphrase.
